data.cenit-community-engagements#CENIT Commun:
The JEDI
thrust of CENIT  is seeking community-partners to accomplish three goals:
(1) understand the challenges and limitations faced by different communities of users in terms of accessing
the internet and other digital networks,
(2) understand the needs and goals of different communities of users in terms of digital accessibility,
and once user needs are well-understood (3) test potential technological solutions and service delivery models
that address these gaps and needs and solicit community feedback to ensure appropriate fit of these technologies.
The followings are some of the ways that we’ve built partnerships so far:
June 2026-present: Prof. Lindsay M. Montgomery
developed a collaboration with Picuris Pueblo and Terentia,
a cloud-based software company in Toronto that provides digital asset management to Tribal Nations and Indigenous communities.
The ongoing community-engaged project centers on the construction of web-based collections managements system and digital workflow
processes grounded in OCAP principles.
January 2026-present: Prof. Lindsay M. Montgomery
developed a collaboration with Dr. Silvia Sarapura-Escobar
(University of Guelph) as part of a larger project entitled “Pathways to Indigenous Food Sovereignty: Integrating Relational Systems
Thinking, Food Environments, and Community Learning Hubs”. The project brings together Indigenous community members from across Canada,
the United States, and Latin America to develop community governed databases that ethically archive traditional ecological
knowledge and foodways. A key component of the collaboration involves enhancing community access to these platforms and building
digital literacy among partners.

He received his Ph.D. in Computer Engineering from the University of California, Santa Cruz, USA, in 2021. Prior to joining the University of Tabuk, he gained research and industry experience at Futurewei, Arista Networks, and Nokia. His research interests include transport protocols, information-centric networking, and networking for emerging and distributed applications.

Tsung Jen (Charles) Hsieh is a Master of Applied Science (MASc) student in the CENIT Research Group, where he focuses on the development and analysis of routing protocols within autonomous systems. He earned his Bachelor of Applied Science (BASc) degree with High Honours in Computer Engineering from the University of Toronto, with minor in Artificial Intelligence Engineering and certificate in Engineering Business. His emphasis is on the design and analysis of shortest-path routing protocols that are loop-free at every instance even in the midst of network changes.

Dr. Ersin Uzun is the Katherine Johnson Executive Director of the ESL Global Cybersecurity Institute and a Professor in the Golisano College of Computing and Information Sciences at the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT). Before joining RIT, he was the Vice President and Director of Computer Science and Systems Sciences Labs at Palo Alto Research Center. His research interests include network/system security, privacy enhancing technologies and human factors in security privacy.
Professor Uzun has M.S. and PhD degrees in computer science from University of California, Irvine and inductee of its Engineering and Computer Science Hall of Fame. He has over 200 global patents and research publications to date and been a PI/Co-PI on many projects sponsored by government agencies (NSF, DARPA, DoD, DoE, OTF, NSA), non-profits (e.g., Google Foundation, Omidyar Networks, ESL Foundation) and corporations (e.g., Lenovo, IBM, Samsung, Google, Sandvik, NBC, Daikin, Hitachi, P&G, Boeing) .

J.J. Garcia-Luna-Aceves joined ECE in 2023 as Professor of ECE and Canada Excellence Research Chair at the University of Toronto. He is a Distinguished Professor Emeritus at the University of California, Santa Cruz (UCSC), and a Visiting Professor at the Computing Research Center of the National Polytechnic Institute in Mexico City, Mexico.
He received the B.S. degree in Electrical Engineering from the Universidad Iberoamericana, Mexico City, Mexico in 1977; and the M.S. and PhD degrees in Electrical Engineering from the University of Hawaii at Manoa, Honolulu, HI in 1980 and 1983, respectively.
Professor Garcia-Luna-Aceves has been a Principal Scientist at the Palo Alto Research Center (PARC), a Center Director at SRI International (SRI) in Menlo Park, California, a Visiting Professor at Sun Laboratories in Menlo Park, California, and a Principal of Protocol Design at Nokia in Mountain View, California. He has served as the Inaugural Chair of the ACM Special Interest Group on Multimedia and as General Chair of numerous conferences, including IEEE MASS 2023, IEEE ICNC 2016, ACM MSWIM 2015, ACM MobiCom 2008, IEEE SECON 2005, ACM Multimedia ’93 and ACM SIGCOMM ’88. He has also served as Program Chair of ACM MobiHoc 2002, ACM MobiCom 2000, IEEE MULTIMEDIA ’92, ACM SIGCOMM ’87 and ACM SIGCOMM ’86. He has been a keynote speaker at numerous conferences.
Professor Garcia-Luna-Aceves’s research focuses on computer communication and covers network architectures, communication protocols, distributed algorithms, digital infrastructures and performance analysis. He holds 76 US patents and has published more than 500 papers in journals, conferences and books. According to Google Scholar, his published work has received more than 44,000 citations and  his h-index is currently 105. He has directed more than 40 PhD theses and more than 40 M.S. theses. At UCSC, he directed the Computer Communication Research Group (CCRG) for 30 years, served as the Department Chair of the Computer Engineering Department and the Computer Science and Engineering Department, and also served as Campus Director of CITRIS and the Banatao Institute.

Prof. Jorg Liebeherr is a Professor in the Edward S. Rogers Sr. Department of
Electrical & Computer Engineering (ECE) at the University of Toronto.
For more than 30 years, he has conducted research in the area of
computer communication networks. His current research interests include
the characterization of network traffic of distributed machine learning
and low-cost sensor networks for environmental monitoring. He holds a
PhD degree in Computer Science from the Georgia Institute of Technology.
He is a Fellow of the IEEE.

Katia Obraczka is Professor of Computer Science and Engineering at UC Santa Cruz. Before joining UCSC, she was a research Scientist at USC’s Information Sciences Institute (ISI) and had a joint faculty appointment at USC’s Computer Science Department. Professor Obraczka’s research interests span the areas of computer networks, distributed systems, and Internet information systems. Her current research focuses on designing and developing protocol architectures motivated by the Internets of the future including wireless networks, IoT, sensor networks, and disruption-tolerant networks. She has been a principal investigator (PI) and a co-PI in a number of projects sponsored by government agencies (e.g., NSF, DARPA, NASA, ARO, DoE, AFOSR) as well as industry (e.g., Cisco, Google, Nokia). She is currently serving as Associate Editor for the IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing as well as ACM Letters in Computer Science. She is a Fellow of the IEEE and has received the Santander Chair of Excellence 2020–2021 and the INRIA International Chair 2021–2026 awards. Prof. Obraczka is the current UCSC CITRIS Campus Director and the Associate Provost of Crown College at UCSC.

Lindsay M. Montgomery is an Associate Professor of Anthropology and Indigenous Studies at the University of Toronto St. George campus.  She holds a B.A. (cum laude) in Human Rights & Anthropology from Columbia University and a PhD in Anthropology from Stanford University. Her research and teaching draws on feminist, collaborative, and anti-colonial approaches to documenting long-term land use practices and histories of inter-ethnic interaction in the American West.

Marcelo M. Carvalho is an Assistant Professor in the Ingram School of Engineering at Texas State University, where he directs the Sustainable High-Performing Intelligent Networks (SHINe) lab. Dr. Carvalho received his Ph.D. degree in Computer Engineering from the University of California, Santa Cruz, in 2006. His research interests are in the areas of wireless and mobile networks, Internet of Things, AI/ML-based networking technologies, and multimedia streaming for AR/VR/XR applications. Currently, he serves as a Vice-Chair of IEEE ComSoc, Central Texas Chapter, and as a Faculty Advisor of the IEEE Mu Upsilon Eta Kappa Nu Chapter (MY-HKN) at Texas State University.

Mahdi’s research focuses on decentralized wireless networks and next-generation multiple access protocols for future communication systems. His work studies how wireless users can share the channel efficiently without centralized scheduling, with the goal of improving effective throughput, reliability, and scalability in increasingly distributed and connected networks.
Michela Meo is a professor at the department of Electronics and Telecommunications, Politecnico di Torino universirty in Italy.

Dr Mohamed Chahine Ghanem is an Associate Professor and Cyber Security Research Lead at Keele University (UK), and a Visiting Associate Professor in Cyber Security and AI within the Cybersecurity Institute at the University of Liverpool. He also holds a Senior Advisor position in Cyber Resilience within the banking sector. Before joining academia, Dr Ghanem built a strong industry foundation with over 15 years of practice in senior positions across law enforcement and corporations, including as Global Cyber Security Auditing Director for Kroll LLC and Nationwide Bank. He holds an Engineering Degree in Computer Systems from EMP (Algeria), an MSc in Digital Forensics & IT Security, and a PhD in Cyber Security Engineering from City, University of London. Dr Ghanem is a Senior Fellow of the Higher Education Academy (SFHEA), holds an MA in Academic Practice, and has earned numerous respected certifications including CISSP, CPCI, multiple GIAC credentials, and the Digital Forensics ACE & XRY qualifications. He currently leads a research programme in applied AI for cyber security and supervises research students working on digital forensics, IoT security, offensive cyber security, and applied AI, with a record of publications in Q1 journals. Dr Ghanem is also a regular keynote speaker at leading international cyber security conferences. He is Editor-in-Chief of the Journal of Cyber Security and Risk Auditing (Q1), an Editor with ACM Digital Threats: Research and Practice, and a Guest Editor and Reviewer for leading cybersecurity venues including JCP, IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security (TIFS), and Elsevier Computers & Security.

data: Mohammadreza is a PhD student in Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Toronto, supervised by Prof. J.J. Garcia-Luna-Aceves. His research focuses on security for routing protocols in computer networks, with an interest in applying cryptographic techniques to build verifiable and trustworthy network infrastructure.Prior to the University of Toronto, he completed his Master's in Information Technology Engineering at École de technologie supérieure (Université du Québec), where his work focused on robust federated learning and blockchain-based credential revocation. He holds a Bachelor's degree in Computer Engineering from Sharif University of Technology.

Dr. Morteza Moghaddassian joined CENIT in 2024 where he is currently a Senior Research Associate.
Prior to CENIT, Morteza has been a post-doctoral fellow in the Network Architecture Lab (NAL) at the Univerity of Toronto.
Morteza holds a PhD in Electrical and Computer engineering from the University of Toronto and his research interests
include network security for the current and the future Internet, communication protocols, network architectures,
cryptography, and the Internet of Things systems, protocols, and applications.
He is an ACM Professional member and a member of IEEE Computer and Communication Societies.

Mostafa Ammar is a Regents' Professor with the School of Computer Science at the Georgia Institute of Technology. He served as Associate Chair of the School of Computer Science from 2006 to 2012. Dr. Ammar received the S.B. and S.M. degrees from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Ph.D. degree from the University of Waterloo, Ontario, Canada.Dr. Ammar's research interests are in network architectures, protocols and services. He has contributions in the areas of multicast communication and services, multimedia streaming, content distribution networks, network simulation, disruption-tolerant networks, and most recently, in mobile cloud computing and network virtualization. He has published extensively in these areas. Over the years he has received funding for his research from federal and defense agencies and national and local industries including NSF, DARPA, AFOSR, ARL, CISCO, IBM, Intel, BellSouth and Sprint. To date, 35 PhD students have completed their degrees under his supervision; many have gone on to distinguished careers in academia and industry. He is the co-author of the textbook "Fundamentals of Telecommunication Networks" published by Wiley-Interscience in 1994.Dr. Ammar has served the networking research community in multiple roles. Most notably, he served as the Editor-in-Chief of the IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking (ToN) from 1999 to 2003, and he was the co-TPC Chair for the IEEE ICNP 1997, ACM CoNEXT 2006 and ACM SIGMETRICS 2007 conferences. He currently serves on the steering committee of the IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing. His awards include the IBM Faculty Partnership Award (1996), Best Paper Award at the 7th WWW conference (1998), the GT Outstanding Doctoral Thesis Advisor Award (2006) and the Outstanding Service Award from the IEEE Technical Committee on Computer Communications (2010), the ACM Mobihoc Best Paper Award (2012), College of Computing Faculty Mentor Award (2015) and the GT Course Survey Teaching Effectiveness Award (2013, 2014, 2015, and 2016).Dr. Ammar was elected Fellow of the IEEE in 2002 and Fellow of the ACM in 2003.

Philip is an Assistant Professor, Teaching Stream and Dean's Advisor for Black Inclusivity in the
Faculty of Applied Science and Engineering at the University of Toronto,
where he is affiliated with Institute for Studies in Transdisciplinary Engineering Education and Practice,
the Division of Engineering Science, and (by courtesy)

His research interests are in the intersection of people and technology, and currently approaches this work

He is a Licensed Professional Engineer in Ontario.

Rolando Menchaca-Méndez is a Professor and founder of the Network and Data Science Laboratory at the Center for Computing Research of the National Polytechnic Institute (CIC-IPN), Mexico. He received his Ph.D. in Computer Engineering from the University of California, Santa Cruz, in 2009. He is the recipient of the 1999 ANIEI Best Mexican Master's Thesis Award, co-recipient of the IEEE MASS 2008 Best Paper Award, and coauthor of the Spotlight Paper for the August 2012 issue of IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing.
Dr. Menchaca-Méndez has published over 150 research papers in journals, conferences, and books. His current research interests include combinatorial optimization, reinforcement learning, graph neural networks, and network protocols for IoT and Smart Cities. A member of the Mexican National System of Researchers and former CIO of the Mexican Ministry of Public Administration, he takes great pride in his growing network of alumni, which includes 13 Ph.D. and 57 M.S. graduates.

data: Dr. Sardana Nikolaeva is a postdoctoral fellow with the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering of the University of Toronto. Her current work with the CENIT project focuses on the socio-technical dynamics of the digital divide, particularly among Indigenous peoples, and developing community research partnerships. Previously, she served as an inaugural postdoctoral fellow of Ziibiing Lab (Global Indigenous Politics Collaboratory) at the Department of Political Science. Sardana holds a PhD in Education from the University of Pittsburgh and a PhD in Cultural Anthropology from the University of Manitoba. Her research interests include Indigenous politics, extractivism, inequities in the Indigenous Arctic, epistemic violence and Indigenous research ethics.

Prof. Dr. Sebastian Rieger is a Professor of Multimedia Communication Networks at Fulda University of Applied Sciences, Germany, where he leads the MMNet research group in the Department of Applied Computer Science. He has held this professorship since 2012, following research and management positions at the Steinbuch Centre for Computing (SCC) at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) and at the Gesellschaft für wissenschaftliche Datenverarbeitung (GWDG) in Göttingen, where he worked on identity management, network and system management, and streaming media in wireless networks. He received his doctorate from the Institute for Information Systems at the University of Göttingen in 2007, with a dissertation on unified authentication in heterogeneous IT infrastructures for secure eScience environments.
His current research interests include network digital twins, resilient inter-domain routing, green intent-based service-aware routing, network services for local AI, and AI-augmented network automation and management. He teaches courses on computer networks and services as well as cloud computing at Fulda University of Applied Sciences, and his group's work is regularly presented at international networking conferences. He is a reviewer for IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management (TNSM) and IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking (TNET).
Selected Recent Work:
Papers on Network Digital Twins, resilient BGP, and intent-based routing at IEEE/IFIP CNSM, IEEE/IFIP NOMS, IRTF NMRG and IFIP Networking
Public open source projects: DigSiNet / DigSiViz (network digital twin verification, visualization, and what-if analysis), learn-sdn-hub (virtual lab for programmable network education and experimentation)

Sheideh Homayon is a PhD candidate at the University of California, Santa Cruz, where her research focuses on wireless networks, medium access control (MAC) protocols, and network simulation. Her work centers on the design and evaluation of MAC-layer protocols through detailed simulation-based analysis. She holds a master's degree from the University of California, Santa Cruz, and a bachelor's degree in computer software engineering from Allameh Mohaddes Nouri University in Iran. Her research aims to advance the performance and efficiency of next-generation wireless communication systems.

Tailai Song received his Ph.D. in Electrical, Electronics and Communications Engineering under the supervision of Prof. Michela Meo and Prof. Marco Mellia from Politecnico di Torino, Italy, in 2026. He is a member of the SmartData@Polito Research Center and the Telecommunication Networks Group. He also received his B.Sc. in Automotive Engineering and M.Sc. in ICT for Smart Societies from Politecnico di Torino in 2020 and 2022, respectively. His research lies at the intersection of computer networks, communication systems, cybersecurity, and artificial intelligence. He has authored more than 15 papers published in established international conferences and journals.

data.ion-intent-oriented-networking#ION: Inte: We study networking technologies to allow end users and processes to state the intent of what service the Internet or a network infrastructure should provide for them with a high-level description, enable the network to automatically map user requirements to performance and policy criteria, and have the network deliver the best performance that satisfies user requirements taking into account network conditions.

data:
A major goal in CENIT is to develop knowledge necessary for creating just and equitable digital infrastructures (JEDI).
To achieve this goal, the research program will approach the work in a way that is socio-economically aware and community-engaged.
The Figure visually represents the method of approach advocated for this research thrust. This research thrust will focus on developing
socio-technical models of intelligent information infrastructures and use that to inform the development of novel network
architectures and protocols that enable just and equitable digital infrastructures. The model would capture end-user needs and factors
affecting network development, network deployments, and network service availability. Justice and equity would be captured in terms of
the extent to which an instantiation of network deployment and service availability meets the needs of users. This model would help in
explaining the current imbalance between user needs and available service and the current digital divide.
It would also provide a framework for development and preliminary assessment of requirements for future networks that address
these current challenges.

data.mints-manifest-based-internet-transport-: We study a clean-slate redesign of the way in which remote processes of digital infrastructures communicate over the Internet and computer networks to support end-user applications and services. The proposed research focuses on eliminating the need for end-to-end connections to support reliable communication, making end-to-end reliable communication efficient for any type of bandwidth-delay product, enabling multipoint services without the need to adopt complex routing protocols, and enabling the Internet itself to serve as an intelligent and secure memory layer for all end-user applications and services.

data.swan-self-reliant-and-wise-ad-hoc-networ: We study the use of machine learning and use results from the other research thrusts to enable self-reliant networks that provide fair and efficient use of shared wireless bandwidth taking into account the connectivity and past history of interference caused by node transmissions. Our research aims to eliminate the current limitations of wireless networks based on such standards as WiFi and 5G.

data.obgp-router#OBGP Router:
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is used for routing across Autonomous Systems (ASes) and is therefore a core component of the Internet.
However, BGP's path-vector dynamics, combined with conflicting policies, can lead to persistent oscillations.
In operational networks, these effects are often mitigated rather than eliminated, typically through suppression mechanisms.
While such measures can reduce route churn, they can also delay convergence.
As routing tables and route churn grow, this overhead becomes increasingly costly in terms of memory and processing resources.
Recent work further shows that these instabilities can be weaponized.
In particular, transitive communities allow an adversary to trigger remote policy changes several hops away.
By forcing distant routers to lower their Local Preference or prepend AS paths, an attacker can induce preference cycles and persistent oscillations.Our recent work on the Ordered Path Etiquette for Routing Algebra (OPERA) and OPERA-based BGP (OBGP) has shown that BGP can,
in theory, be made stable and loop-free without changing BGP signaling by imposing suitable ordering constraints on route import,
selection, and export. However, no prior work had implemented and experimentally validated OBGP in a routing daemon.The contributions of our research are:
The first implementation of OBGP in the widely used open-source GoBGP daemon.
A Kubernetes-based emulation environment and experimental tooling for fill and drain experiments.
An experimental comparison between OBGP and unmodified GoBGP on germany50, BAD GADGET, and an adapted noble-eu topology,
reporting convergence and Loc-RIB characteristics.
Our research shows that OBGP can be integrated into a widely used BGP daemon without changing BGP signaling,
and that the resulting system behaves as predicted by prior theory.
Our work provides the first daemon-level validation of OPERA-based BGP in a widely used routing daemon without changing BGP signaling.
The central result is that a routing design previously established only in theory can be brought into an operational routing system
without sacrificing interoperability or local policy control.
Our GoBGP implementation shows this concretely: under cyclic policies, it eliminates persistent oscillation, converges, and
reduces control-plane state. In this sense, the contribution is not only an implementation of a known design,
but a validation that the design holds up in a real routing stack.
This gives the field a concrete baseline for future work.
The next step is to extend that baseline from plain paths to structured path objects, from single-path export to ordered path sets,
and from one-dimensional ranking to richer routing algebras.More details on our research are presented in our paper "Making BGP-4 More Efficient and Oscillation-Free."To facilitate reproducibility and foster further research, the source code of the modified GoBGP daemon,
the emulation environment, and the experimental raw data are available at
Router GitHub
and
here.This work was supported by a fellowship of the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD) and by the Canada Excellence Research Chair
in Intelligent Digital Infrastructures at the University of Toronto, funded by the Tri-agency Institutional Programs Secretariat.
